newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Kapuni decision brings competition to gas - NZPA.
newsitem.headline: Kapuni decision brings competition to gas - NZPA.

text.p: A High Court decision dividing NZ$1.2 billion worth of gas between the Fletcher Challenge group and the Shell-Todd partnership would bring long-overdue competition to the gas industry, Todd Petroleum Mining managing director Richard Tweedie said on Wednesday.
"This does mean that we will see some competition at long last in the gas market," he told the New Zealand Press Association.

In a reserved decision, Justice Sir Ian Barker and lay adviser Gaire Blunt said the original 1967 contract between the Kapuni partners -- Shell, Todd Petroleum and BP -- and the government, did not expire after its initial 25 year term.
The contract required the parties to negotiate in good faith on the future prices and minimum quantities of remaining gas expected to be available for at least 15 years.

However, Justice Barker also ruled that since the contract was likely to substantially lessen competition in the gas market in breach of the Commerce Act, more gas should be allowed into the market through another supplier.
"As from 1 April 1997, the remainder of the gas in the Kapuni field is to be divided equally between the plaintiffs and the defendants," he said.
Tweedie said the decision was not an outright victory as the contract remained intact and a price now had to negotiated for up to 350 petajoules of gas estimated in the field.
He declined to put a value on the gas, saying that was dependent on where it could be sold, but other commentators have said the total extra gas could be worth up to NZ$1.2 billion.

"We've lost some of the ancillary legal arguments around the contract and there will have to be some work done on issues around that, but on the big substantive issue I think we have done reasonably well," Tweedie said.
The Kapuni field was discovered in 1957 and in 1967 the Crown established the Natural Gas Corporation (NGC) to buy and process the gas.
In 1988, Fletcher Challenge acquired NGC as part of its purchase of state-owned Petrocorp.
He said the decision would cut about $15 million a year from Fletcher Energy's earnings before interest and tax, but that was within the company's expectations.
"Taking the outcome in totality, we're fairly content with the way it's turned out," he told NZPA.
Kapuni has supplied 22 petajoules of gas annually for the past three years, the bulk of which has been sold to the Methanex petrochemical plants in Taranaki and to Bay of Plenty Fertiliser.

The parties have debated the issue for the past four years. Last year Shell-Todd took the issue to court, saying the exclusive purchasing rights of Kapuni Gas Contracts -- a Fletcher Challenge subsidiary -- expired after 25 years, enabling Shell-Todd to sell the gas elsewhere.
Failing that, Shell-Todd claimed the contract breached the Commerce Act and was no longer enforceable.

Fletcher Challenge spokesman Barry Akers today declined to comment on the likelihood of an appeal by the company, but said the court's endorsement of the 1967 contract was a "significant positive" for the company.
NGC, one-third owned by Fletcher Challenge, is responsible for managing Kapuni Gas Contracts' gas operation. It sells LPG and natural gasoline from the gas back to Shell-Todd.

NGC took about 2.7 PJ of gas from Kapuni in the year ended June 1996, but has previously anticipated meeting about a quarter of its gas needs post-2004 with Kapuni gas. Today the company declined to comment saying the judgement was a complex one.

Justice Barker ruled that Kapuni Gas Contracts would be entitled to 11PJ to 16PJ of gas annually, depending on production from the field, but that it would first have to meet its obligations to its petrochemical customers, possibly from its Maui gas entitlements.
Shell-Todd would be free to sell their share of the gas where they liked, but not for petrochemical use nor for generation of electricity other than through industrial co-generation.

While finding the 1967 contract lessened competition, Ju stice Barker said it had not been proved the Fletcher Challenge related companies had used their dominant position in the market to prevent Shell-Todd competing in the market.
Because of the anti-competitive nature of the contract, Justice Barker declined to award compensation to the defendants and rejected their suggestion that the excess gas be offered for tender.
-- Wellington Newsroom (64-4-4734746)
